column3: Our dog sat in Dad's chair. He wore Dad's new hat, and his brown ears hung down like wet socks. On the table, an empty plate lay beside some cake on the floor. Dad stood in the doorway with a cup of tea. His mouth was open. The dog looked very happy. It was a good birthday, for one of them.
column4: Mr Bell's garden was ready for the party. Paper birds hung from the trees, and little sandwiches stood in perfect rows. In the middle of the grass, his white cat lay across the big chocolate cake. Its eyes were closed. A pink flower from the cake rested on its head. It looked like a little pink hat.
column5: At the school concert, everything glittered except the king's crown, which was made from a cereal box. His red coat dragged behind him like a tired carpet. Beside the throne stood a tiny tree with two enormous shoes underneath it. Whenever the tree sneezed, its leaves shook. The king stared straight ahead, determined to rule this kingdom with dignity.
column6: The hotel's breakfast room promised elegance. Silver spoons gleamed on spotless cloths; a pianist murmured something expensive in the corner. Across this polished scene waddled a duck, leaving damp signatures on the marble. Behind it followed the manager, holding a croissant with the strained optimism of a man attempting a diplomatic negotiation. The duck appeared to be considering a better offer.
column7: It was difficult to take the mayor's portrait seriously once the cleaning staff had installed a coat hook beneath his nose. Every winter, damp umbrellas transformed his solemn moustache into a collection of dripping tentacles. The receptionists had stopped noticing. Visitors, however, tended to approach the desk wearing expressions of unusual restraint, as though the dignity of local government depended entirely on their self-control.

column3: My old bike stood by the garden wall. Its seat was too low now, and the red paint was pale. I put my hand on the bell. Once, I loved its little song. Today, my new bike waited by the gate. It was big and blue. I felt happy, but I looked back at the red one for a long time.
column4: My new school jacket hung on the bedroom door. It looked too smart for this room, with its toy cars and football pictures. I checked my bag again. Outside, my friends were calling, but Mum stood beside the window with her camera. I wanted to tell her to stop. Then I saw her smile and stood still for one last photograph.
column5: From the top row of the empty stadium, the pitch looked smaller than I remembered. So did the boy in the old team photograph on my phone. His socks slipped around his ankles; his grin filled half his face. I knew how frightened he had been that day. Tomorrow, I would be choosing the team. The thought made me sit straighter.
column6: Her childhood bedroom had become the place where unwanted things waited: a broken lamp, spare blankets, a printer nobody could persuade to work. Yet the pencil marks recording her height remained beside the door. She traced the highest line with her thumb. At sixteen she had considered it a finish line. Now, home for the summer, she was less certain where anything ended.
column7: At the dinner table, his father had begun asking questions and waiting for the answers. This small alteration unsettled Daniel more than the deepening of his voice. Between them, the familiar objects persisted: chipped jug, folded newspaper, the salt cellar shaped like a hen. Everything looked comfortably unchanged. Yet the silence after each question offered him a space he was learning how to occupy.

column3: Every house on our street is grey. Every door has a number. There are no flowers in the gardens, and the children all wear black. At six, the big screen tells us to go inside. A camera turns above my door. I keep my hand in my pocket. Inside it is a small red flower. I found it by the wall.
column4: At breakfast, the kitchen screen showed our family's score. We had ninety points today, so the water was warm. Across the street, the windows of number eight were dark. Their score was lower. Dad ate without speaking. Beside his plate, his wrist light flashed green each time he smiled at the camera. The bread tasted dry in my mouth.
column5: Nobody looked up at the birds any more. They were government cameras, shaped like sparrows, with little red lights beneath their wings. At lunchtime they gathered above the school gates. Their metal feet clicked against the fence while we waited to be counted. One had a real feather caught in its beak. I watched it until my number was called.
column6: The public garden contained twelve approved species, each identified by a plastic label. Visitors followed arrows between beds of identical flowers while speakers offered advice on healthy thoughts. At the far end, behind a bench, a weed had pushed through the paving. Someone had placed a security cone around it. Two gardeners waited nearby, consulting the regulations before deciding what to do.
column7: Silence was the district's most expensive privilege. Behind the glass frontage of the Quiet Club, members sipped coffee without advertisements addressing them by name. Outside, the pavement screens brightened as pedestrians approached, interpreting hesitation as interest and exhaustion as consent. A woman paused beneath the club's awning. For three seconds, its shadow concealed her face from the nearest camera. She closed her eyes.

column3: On a green hill stood a tiny house. Its roof was red, and its windows shone like stars. A white rabbit sat by the door in a little blue coat. Behind the house grew a tree with golden apples. One apple fell each morning. The rabbit put it in a basket for the poor girl who lived down the hill.
column4: Deep in the wood stood a mill with a silver wheel. It turned even when the river was dry. Inside, a small woman made flour from moonlight, and the air smelled of warm cakes. Three empty bowls waited on her table. Above them hung a sign: one meal for a kind word. The richest king could buy nothing there.
column5: Beyond the thorn hedge, the princess's garden lay beneath a hundred years of snow. Roses slept inside clear ice, and silver fish hung motionless in the frozen pond. Only the gardener's little hut was warm. From its crooked chimney rose a thread of smoke. Whoever brought spring back to the garden would find the lost crown beneath the first flower.
column6: Each winter, the mountain gave the village a single ruby. It appeared in the snow outside the poorest household, warm enough to melt a small circle around itself. That year, the mayor had built a hut beside the summit and dressed his servants in rags. Below him, in a room without a chimney, a child slept beneath a steadily brightening blanket.
column7: There was once a kingdom where every broken promise became a stone. Pebbles crowded the market square; boulders blocked the palace gates. Eventually, even the roads disappeared beneath the weight of what people had sworn to do. Only the shoemaker's daughter could walk freely through the streets. Around her bare feet, the stones softened into moss, and the tired earth began to breathe again.

column3: Dad's coat hangs by the door. One pocket has a hole, and a button is missing. He wears it to work every day. In winter, the coat smells of rain. In summer, it smells of warm dust. Sometimes, I hide my hands inside its big sleeves. Dad laughs, and the sound comes through the thick cloth.
column4: The woman at the bus stop held a bag of oranges. One had fallen out and lay beside her shoe. She watched the road without moving. Rain made small circles in the water near the pavement. I picked up the orange and gave it back. For a moment, her tired face changed. Then she looked down the road again.
column5: After the furniture went, the flat sounded different. Every step returned from the walls a little louder than before. Pale squares showed where photographs had kept the wallpaper from fading. In the kitchen, I found a spoon behind the radiator. Its handle was bent. Such a small, ordinary thing, yet I wrapped it carefully before putting it in my bag.
column6: The laundrette was almost empty. A man's blue shirt turned behind a round window, lifting one sleeve as if making a slow, uncertain greeting. Beside me, an elderly woman folded a child's jumper across her knees. She smoothed it twice, although it needed neither fold nor smoothing. Outside, a bus pulled away. We both looked up, then returned to our separate tasks.
column7: Only after her mother moved out did Leena notice how the kitchen light changed towards evening. It gathered on the worn patch of table where vegetables had been chopped for thirty years, revealing grooves too shallow for a fingertip to follow. She had intended to replace the table. Now she stood beside it, holding the catalogue, while the room quietly complicated her plans.

column3: Grandma's kitchen is always warm. Bread sits on the table, and the yellow cups sing when she fills them with tea. Their songs are quiet and sweet. Grandma likes the blue cup best because it sings her mother's song. She drinks slowly by the window. Outside, the buses come and go, and people hurry to work in the rain.
column4: Rain fell inside our house every Sunday. Mum put buckets beside the sofa, and Dad moved his newspaper away from the wet chair. The kitchen stayed dry, so we ate there. After lunch, my sister sailed paper boats across the living room. By evening, everything was dry again. On Monday, Mum took the buckets back to the cupboard under the stairs.
column5: The postman carried winter in his coat pockets. Whenever he reached for a letter, a few snowflakes drifted onto the doorstep, even in July. My mother kept a towel beside the door for him. During the hottest weeks, neighbours asked him to stay for tea. He sat carefully in their kitchens, leaving small, shining puddles beneath his chair.
column6: Every August, the sea came up the hill to visit my aunt. It slipped beneath her front door, carrying the smell of salt and a few embarrassed crabs. She rolled up the carpet and set out a basin for the smallest fish. By morning it had gone, leaving shells in the umbrella stand and her late husband's footprints beside the bed.
column7: When Elena's father lost his memory, the names he forgot began appearing on the walls of his flat. They emerged beneath the wallpaper in his careful handwriting, swelling the paper like roots beneath a pavement. Each morning she copied them into a notebook before making his breakfast. He ate contentedly beside the window, surrounded by people he could no longer remember how to miss.

column3: Grass grows through the road outside our house. The shops are empty, and birds live in the old bus. We get water from the river now. In the school garden, Dad grows food. He puts beans in my old classroom by the window. Their leaves are green and bright. I like the room better with something living in it.
column4: The supermarket roof was open to the sky. Rain filled the empty shelves, and a young tree grew beside the broken till. We walked slowly between fallen boxes. Even the tins were empty now. Then, near the back door, I saw a bird sitting in a shoe. Four tiny mouths opened beneath its warm brown body. We left very quietly.
column5: From the motorway bridge, we could see the city we had avoided for years. Trees crowded the streets, pushing their branches through office windows. A bright strip of washing hung between two ruined towers. Someone was living there. Below us, among the rusting cars, a narrow path had been cleared. Fresh bicycle tracks marked the mud at its entrance.
column6: The cinema still advertised a film that nobody alive remembered seeing. Beneath the torn poster, our settlement's repair shop occupied the old foyer. Bicycle chains hung where tickets had once been sold, and seedlings filled a popcorn machine. Each evening, sunlight entered through the collapsed roof and lit the blank screen. Children sat facing it while the elders told their stories.
column7: Spring exposed what winter had spared us: the buckled rails, the drowned orchards, the houses leaning towards the river as though listening for an explanation. We planted potatoes above the flood line. Across the valley, another settlement answered our morning smoke with its own, a thin grey thread rising through the blossom. For the first time in years, distance suggested company rather than danger.

column3: The sky was under my bed today. Blue clouds moved between my shoes, and a small sun warmed the floor. I opened the window. Outside, a fish rode a bicycle along the street. Its bell made the sound of my name. At the corner, the houses sat down. They looked tired. I put a blanket over the smallest one.
column4: Our dining room was full of sand. A large clock lay on the table, slowly turning into soup. Each time it made a sound, another spoon appeared beside my plate. Through the window, I watched the moon walk down the road in my father's shoes. It stopped outside the baker's shop and waited for a loaf of warm bread.
column5: Halfway up the stairs, the steps became piano keys. My shoes played a tune I almost recognised. At the top waited a door with an enormous ear instead of a handle. Behind it, the sea was having an argument with a wardrobe. Every angry wave brought another coat sliding beneath the door, its empty sleeves reaching towards my feet.
column6: The city had folded itself into an envelope. Along its creases, buses balanced like insects, while commuters squeezed between the teeth of a silver zip. I recognised my street by the smell of burnt toast escaping from a stamp. Somewhere inside the paper, a woman was ironing a thunderstorm. With each stroke, the sky above her became a little smoother.
column7: At the museum of unfinished afternoons, visitors surrendered their shadows in exchange for teaspoons. The galleries contained only distances: the space between a question and its answer, the remaining length of a farewell. In the final room, an enormous eyelid opened across the ceiling. Beneath it, a child watered a row of empty chairs, which were beginning, reluctantly, to remember being trees.

column3: The swing in our garden was still. Yellow leaves lay on its small wooden seat. My brother loved that swing. He pushed his feet up towards the sky and laughed. Now his red boots stood by the back door, clean and empty. Mum looked out of the kitchen window. Her tea was cold. Nobody went into the garden that day.
column4: By morning, the flood water was gone. Our little house stood in deep brown mud, with its front door wide open. A family photograph lay beside the gate. Brown mud covered half the faces. Dad held my hand while we waited for news of my sister. On the roof, her blue scarf moved gently in the warm, bright wind.
column5: Nobody had cleared her place at the breakfast table. The toast was hard, the butter soft in the sunlight. From the open window came the ordinary sounds of Saturday: a lawnmower, a neighbour laughing, children chasing a ball. I stared at the little pot of jam she had opened. Its lid lay beside her plate, ready for a hand that would never return.
column6: The wedding flowers arrived three days after the accident. Unable to refuse them, her father arranged the white roses in every vase he could find. Their perfume filled the hallway and climbed the stairs. In her bedroom, the dress still hung beneath its thin cover, one sleeve extended slightly, as though she had been interrupted while reaching for something.
column7: At the station, his mother's suitcase remained beside the bench where he had persuaded her to wait. Her gloves lay across its handle, fingertips touching with a neatness that seemed unbearable. Announcements dissolved beneath the vaulted roof; departures proceeded with mechanical courtesy. He had returned with the tickets and two cups of coffee. One was still too hot to hold.

column3: Dust blew along the town's wide street. A brown horse stood outside the bank, moving its ears at every sound. Across the road, two men sat in the shade. Their boots were white with dust. Behind them, the shop doors were open. I could smell coffee and hot bread. Beyond the last house, the dry land went on for miles.
column4: The cattle stood close together by the river. Their dark backs shone in the evening light, and flies moved around their eyes. On the far bank, a rider watched from a tired grey horse. His hat hid most of his face. Behind him stretched the open plain. Smoke rose from our campfire, carrying the smell of coffee into the cooling air.
column5: By midday, the little station was a square of shade in a hundred miles of heat. A water barrel stood beneath the roof, its wooden sides dark with damp. Beyond the tracks, grass moved across the plain like ripples on a pond. The stationmaster leaned against his office door. Far away, a thin thread of smoke marked the approaching train.
column6: Wind pushed dust through the unfinished church, gathering it in the corners where pews would eventually stand. Outside, horses stamped beside a wagon loaded with timber. The new town had a bank, three saloons and no school. From the ridge, it looked temporary: a scattering of pale boards set against the enormous patience of the land. Yet somebody had already planted roses.
column7: The abandoned ranch appeared at sunset, its windmill turning with a complaint that travelled astonishingly far through the stillness. Beneath the loading rails, cattle had worn a shallow hollow in the earth; now it held last night's rain. Ruth dismounted and loosened the saddle. Across the plain, the approaching railway shone briefly, a bright incision in the country her father had called endless.
